\chapter{Synthesis --- Describing Things}
\label{ch:sintesis-describir}
\hlchaptermodality{60}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose ser or estar with an adjective and make it agree.}

I can choose ser or estar with an adjective and make it agree.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — describing things}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-sintesis-describir}



\begin{quote}
Two verbs for \emph{to be}. Which is for what a thing \textbf{is}? (\emph{Ser}.) Which is for how it \textbf{is right now}? (\emph{Estar}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You met \emph{ser} and \emph{estar} as a pair long before this book had a single word to put after them. Now it does, and the pair finally does its job:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{La casa es grande.} & The house is big — that is what it is. \\
\emph{Estoy cansado.} & I am tired — today. \\
\emph{Soy profesor.} & I am a teacher — and no \emph{un}. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three sentences, three different jobs for \emph{to be}, and nothing memorised as a phrase.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which words shift}]
The ending tells you, and you now have one of each:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{shifts?} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\emph{-o} & \textbf{yes} & \emph{cansado} $\to$ \emph{cansada} \\
\emph{-e} & no & \emph{grande} stays \emph{grande} \\
\emph{-ista}, \emph{-ante} & no & \emph{artista}, \emph{estudiante} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So you never have to guess. Look at the last letter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{La casa es grande}
  \item \emph{Estoy cansado} — and mean it
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{Ser} or \emph{estar} for tired? (\emph{\textbf{Estar}}.) Where does the describing word go? (\textbf{After} the noun.) And what tells you whether it shifts? (Its \textbf{last letter}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
